text: Paul's Shipwreck
A storm, a snake, and the road to Rome
The last chapters of the Book of Acts tell of the most dangerous voyage of the Apostle Paul.
Chapter One. A prisoner sails for Rome.
Paul had spent two years under arrest in Caesarea. Governor Festus sent him to be tried by the emperor.
Paul and other prisoners were handed over to a centurion of the Augustan band named Julius.
With Paul sailed Luke, the author of Acts, and Aristarchus of Thessalonica.
Luke writes: we. So he was on this voyage himself.
At Sidon, Julius treated Paul kindly and let him visit his friends.
At Myra in Lycia the centurion found a ship of Alexandria, loaded with wheat and bound for Italy.
Chapter Two. The warning.
Contrary winds held them back. With difficulty they reached a bay in Crete called the Fair Havens.
The Fast. the Day of Atonement. was already past. Autumn had come, the season of storms.
Paul warned them: the voyage would bring great harm, not only to the cargo and the ship, but to their lives.
But the centurion trusted the master and the owner of the ship more than Paul.
They decided to sail on to Phenice, a better harbour to spend the winter.
Chapter Three. Euroclydon.
A gentle south wind blew, and they set out. Then a violent north-east wind struck. Euroclydon.
The ship was caught. They could not bear up into the wind, and let her drive.
They bound the ship with ropes, threw out the cargo, and then the ship's tackle.
For many days neither sun nor stars appeared. All hope of being saved was taken away.
By night an angel of God stood by Paul.
Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee.
There shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship.
Chapter Four. The shipwreck.
On the fourteenth night the sailors sensed land was near, and cast four anchors out of the stern.
In the dark they tried to escape in the boat and leave everyone behind.
Paul told the centurion: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.
The soldiers cut the ropes of the boat, and let her fall into the sea.
Before dawn Paul urged them all to eat: not a hair would fall from anyone's head.
He took bread, gave thanks to God in the presence of them all, broke it, and began to eat.
There were two hundred and seventy-six people on board.
At daybreak the ship ran aground. The bow stuck fast, and the waves broke the stern apart.
The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wishing to save Paul, stopped them.
And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land.
Chapter Five. The island of Melita.
The island was called Melita. Today it is Malta, south of Sicily.
The islanders showed them great kindness and lit a fire, for it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered sticks and laid them on the fire. A viper came out of the heat and fastened on his hand.
The islanders said: this man must be a murderer. But Paul shook it off into the fire and felt no harm.
Publius, the chief man of the island, received Paul and his companions for three days.
Paul prayed, laid his hands on Publius's sick father, and healed him.
After this, others on the island who had diseases came, and were healed.
Chapter Six. Rome.
Three months later they sailed on a ship of Alexandria named Castor and Pollux. to Syracuse, Rhegium and Puteoli.
At Puteoli they found Christian brothers. After seven days Paul set out for Rome along the Appian Way.
The Christians of Rome came out to meet him as far as Appii Forum and the Three Taverns.
Whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage.
In Rome Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier who guarded him.
He called the Jews of Rome and spoke of the Kingdom of God from morning till evening. Some believed, some did not.
Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
For two whole years he lived in Rome and received all who came. From here he wrote his epistles.
Here the Book of Acts ends. According to Church tradition, Paul died a martyr in Rome in the year sixty-seven.
